purpose: Guide analysts in assigning slider values consistently across future and historical presidential elections.

scoringPrinciple.coreRule: Each slider measures stress against the White House party unless it is in the Opposition Threat Offset section, which subtracts stress by making the challenger less acceptable.

scoreMeaning.low: Present but weak, narrow, or not electorally central
scoreMeaning.high: Dominant feature of the election environment
scoreMeaning.max: Historically severe or defining feature of the election

doNotScoreBy: whether the analyst agrees with the grievance
whether media elites treated it seriously
whether the issue was morally important but electorally invisible
isolated anecdotes without broader political force
scoreBy: whether the factor plausibly changed turnout, persuasion, defection, or legitimacy

electoralConversion.14-21: High conversion risk; national preference may not map cleanly to outcome
electoralConversion.22-30: Severe conversion risk; popular mandate and electoral outcome may diverge

democraticConversionRisk.22-30: Catastrophic risk; voter intent may be distorted or overridden

institutionalStress.description: Measures whether the White House party looks structurally stable, unified, and institutionally credible.

guidance.0: White House party gained seats or clearly overperformed in a way that strengthened mandate.
guidance.2: Clear House-seat losses or midterm rebuke, but not catastrophic.
guidance.3: Major midterm repudiation or loss of House control.

2: 2018 Republicans after Democrats took the House

guidance.0: Sitting president is the White House party nominee.
guidance.1: Functional incumbency remains strong despite unusual succession.
guidance.2: Successor has unusually strong continuity with popular incumbent.
guidance.3: Open seat with partial continuity but no direct incumbent advantage.
guidance.4: White House party nominee is not the sitting president and cannot fully inherit incumbency.

2: 1988 George H. W. Bush inheriting Reagan-era legitimacy

guidance.0: Nomination uncontested or party unified early.
guidance.1: Ordinary primary tension with no lasting damage.
guidance.2: Visible factional tension, but party consolidates.
guidance.3: Serious primary conflict, lingering factional resentment, or legitimacy doubts.
guidance.4: Major party rupture, forced nominee change, or convention-level instability.
guidance.5: Severe party fracture with lasting electoral consequences.

2: 2024 Democrats after Biden withdrawal and Harris consolidation
5: 1912 Republicans split between Taft and Roosevelt

guidance.0: No meaningful third-party or independent campaign.
guidance.2: Third-party candidate plausibly affects margins or channels discontent.
guidance.3: Major third-party or independent campaign reshapes election dynamics.

1: 2024 RFK Jr. after collapse/withdrawal impact reduced

guidance.0: No major scandal tied to incumbent administration.
guidance.1: Partisan allegations or minor scandal with limited crossover recognition.
guidance.2: Significant scandal but not defining the election.
guidance.3: Major scandal seriously damages incumbent credibility.
guidance.4: System-defining scandal or legitimacy collapse.

3: 1980 Carter amid broad governance crisis but not Watergate-level scandal

guidance.0: Party elites project confidence and continuity.
guidance.1: Visible elite panic, forced strategic pivot, or public confidence crisis.

formalEconomicStress.description: Measures official macroeconomic stress: recession, unemployment, inflation, GDP, and formal economic trend.

guidance.0: No recession or broad formal contraction during campaign year.
guidance.2: Weak growth or recession fears but no clear recession.
guidance.4: Recent recession or recession-like conditions still politically salient.
guidance.6: Clear recession or economic collapse during election year.

guidance.0: Inflation plus unemployment clearly improves.
guidance.3: Major deterioration.
guidance.4: Dominant election issue; voters experience inflation/unemployment crisis.

guidance.0: Real GDP per capita growth strong or improving.
guidance.2: Growth weak or below recent expectations.
guidance.3: Growth stagnant or declining in politically meaningful way.
guidance.4: Severe contraction or collapse.

guidance.0: Unemployment low or falling.
guidance.1: Low but anxiety or job-quality concerns exist.
guidance.2: Meaningful unemployment rise or weak labor confidence.
guidance.3: High unemployment is central to election.

1: 2016 job-quality/deindustrialization concern despite decent headline unemployment

guidance.0: Inflation low and not politically salient.
guidance.2: Inflation recently severe or still shaping voter memory.
guidance.3: Inflation is a defining grievance of the election.

livedMaterialStress.description: Measures whether voters experience daily life as unaffordable, insecure, downwardly mobile, or insulting despite official indicators.

guidance.0: Most voters feel better off or stable.
guidance.3: Large bloc feels worse off.
guidance.4: Worse-off sentiment is central.
guidance.5: Historically high worse-off sentiment or overwhelming lived dissatisfaction.

guidance.0: Housing not electorally central.
guidance.2: Housing affordability meaningful for some blocs.
guidance.3: Housing/rent burden central for young/working voters.
guidance.4: Housing crisis is a defining material condition.

guidance.0: Food prices not politically salient.
guidance.3: Grocery/food prices are a defining everyday symbol of economic pain.

guidance.0: Debt/healthcare/childcare/credit stress not salient.
guidance.3: Core material grievance shaping voter anger.

guidance.0: Voters broadly believe upward mobility is available.
guidance.2: Young/working voters see major barriers to home, family, or stability.
guidance.3: Blocked future is a defining political mood.

guidance.0: Official economic message matches lived experience.
guidance.1: Some disconnect between official claims and voter experience.
guidance.2: The governing party's economic message feels insulting or detached from daily reality.

legitimacyMoralInjuryStress.description: Measures whether the incumbent party loses moral credibility, coalition trust, or democratic legitimacy even without formal collapse.

guidance.0: No major moral rupture inside incumbent coalition.
guidance.2: Significant issue for one coalition bloc.
guidance.3: Major coalition-level moral conflict.
guidance.4: Dominant moral injury for core base groups.
guidance.5: Defining moral rupture of the election.

3: 2016 donor/elite legitimacy crisis among left/populist blocs

guidance.0: Foreign policy does not split incumbent coalition.
guidance.3: Major split across coalition blocs.
guidance.4: Foreign policy becomes a defining internal rupture.

3: 2004 Iraq Democrats/Republicans conflict as national issue

guidance.0: No visible repression issue.
guidance.2: Recurring repression but limited electoral reach.
guidance.3: Visible repression affects coalition legitimacy.
guidance.4: State/institutional repression is a defining legitimacy crisis.

guidance.0: Base energized or loyal.
guidance.3: Core coalition groups feel betrayed or politically blackmailed.

guidance.0: Party appears responsive to voters.
guidance.2: Strong perception that donors/security/corporate interests dominate.
guidance.3: Donor/state capture is central to anti-incumbent politics.

3: 1896 backlash against finance/corporate power as central cleavage

guidance.0: Official narrative remains plausible to voters.
guidance.1: Elite story visibly conflicts with lived reality.

foreignMilitaryStress.description: Measures direct foreign-policy or military damage to the White House party.

guidance.0: No major foreign/military failure.
guidance.3: Major unresolved foreign-policy failure.
guidance.4: Severe failure or humiliation.

3: 2024 Gaza as foreign-policy failure layer separate from moral injury

guidance.0: No war fatigue.
guidance.3: War fatigue dominates the political environment.

guidance.0: Foreign policy does not undermine domestic moral claims.
guidance.2: Foreign policy directly undermines the incumbent party's moral/democratic claims.

candidateAffectCoalitionFit.description: Measures whether the incumbent-party nominee emotionally and symbolically fits the political moment.

weakCandidate.label: Candidate seen as weak, fake, corrupt, exhausted, or imposed

guidance.0: Candidate has strong affective fit and credibility.
guidance.3: Candidate affect is a major drag.
guidance.4: Candidate is widely experienced as illegitimate, exhausted, fake, corrupt, or imposed.

cantSpeakPain.label: Cannot credibly speak to material pain

guidance.0: Candidate credibly addresses material conditions.
guidance.1: Candidate partially addresses pain but not fully.
guidance.2: Candidate struggles to speak to core pain.
guidance.3: Candidate appears detached or insulting toward material suffering.

guidance.0: Core coalition feels represented.
guidance.3: Core blocs feel betrayed, ignored, or morally coerced.

oppositionThreatOffset.description: Subtracts from incumbent stress when the challenger is scary, unpopular, blamed, chaotic, or unacceptable enough to push voters back to the White House party.

guidance.0: Challenger seen as normal or acceptable.
guidance.3: Large bloc sees challenger as extreme.
guidance.4: Extremism is central to incumbent message.
guidance.5: Challenger widely seen as authoritarian or dangerous.
guidance.6: Opposition threat is historically severe and should strongly help incumbent party.

3: 2012 Romney among Democratic base, but limited broader fear
5: 2020 Trump as incumbent threat for Biden coalition
2024 Trump threat offset helping Democrats somewhat

guidance.0: Challenger personally popular or inspiring.
guidance.3: Clearly unpopular.
guidance.4: Very unpopular.

4: 2016 Trump and Clinton both high-unfavorability, score challenger unpopularity against Trump from Democratic incumbent lens

challengerBlamed.label: Challenger party blamed for prior crisis

guidance.0: Challenger party not blamed for recent crisis.
guidance.3: Meaningful blame for recent crisis.
guidance.4: Strong blame.
guidance.5: Challenger party still heavily blamed for a defining crisis.

0: 2016 Republicans not broadly blamed for incumbent Democratic conditions
3: 2012 Republicans still tied to Bush-era crisis for many voters
5: 2008 Republicans blamed for Bush/crash in reverse as incumbent stress rather than offset

guidance.0: Incumbent base not especially motivated by fear of challenger.
guidance.3: Fear is a major incumbent motivator.
guidance.4: Fear-driven turnout is central to incumbent survival strategy.
guidance.5: Fear of challenger is the dominant incumbent-party turnout force.

guidance.0: Challenger not tied to chaos or scandal.
guidance.3: Major scandal/chaos risk.
guidance.4: Challenger is widely defined by chaos, criminality, scandal, or instability.

4: 2020 Trump for anti-Trump voters, though he was incumbent so score carefully depending on role

electoralCollegeConversion.description: Measures whether national voter preference converts efficiently into Electoral College victory.

guidance.0: Incumbent support efficiently distributed.
guidance.4: Meaningful wasted-vote problem.
guidance.8: Incumbent can win popular vote but plausibly lose Electoral College.

8: 1888 Cleveland-style popular vote/Electoral College split risk

guidance.0: Challenger support inefficient or too narrow.
guidance.4: Meaningful battleground efficiency.
guidance.8: Challenger can lose popular vote and still win Electoral College.

guidance.0: Third-party vote not geographically decisive.
guidance.3: Could plausibly alter several close states.
guidance.4: Strong spoiler effect in decisive geography.

guidance.0: No meaningful regional realignment favoring challenger.
guidance.3: Important regional shift.
guidance.4: Major realignment changes map.
guidance.5: Election is defined by regional realignment.

guidance.0: Popular vote and Electoral College likely align.
guidance.3: High mismatch risk.
guidance.4: Mismatch is central to plausible outcome.

democraticConversionRisk.description: Measures whether voter intent can be distorted, stopped, litigated, suppressed, or overturned by election machinery.

guidance.0: Outcome not dependent on tiny margins.
guidance.1: Some close states but not decisive.
guidance.2: Several states close but outcome has cushion.
guidance.3: Outcome may depend on one or two close states.
guidance.4: Extremely close decisive-state margin likely.
guidance.5: Election hinges on razor-thin margin in decisive state.

guidance.0: No significant ballot access/counting/rejection issue.
guidance.3: Meaningful access or rejection issue in close states.
guidance.4: Major ballot design, purge, rejection, or access problem.
guidance.5: Ballot machinery likely changes or obscures outcome.

5: 2000 Florida butterfly ballots, rejected ballots, recount disputes

guidance.0: Election administration broadly neutral or non-decisive.
guidance.2: Meaningful partisan control in close states.
guidance.3: Partisan actors have direct influence over decisive process.
guidance.4: Partisan administration is central to disputed outcome.

guidance.0: Courts unlikely to affect outcome.
guidance.1: Some lawsuits but low outcome risk.
guidance.3: Court intervention could shape outcome.
guidance.4: Court intervention likely or actually decisive.

guidance.0: No credible certification sabotage pathway.
guidance.3: Serious pressure on certification officials.
guidance.4: Coordinated attempt plausible.
guidance.5: Active attempt to override certified results.

2: 2024 elevated risk due precedent but not realized same way

guidance.0: No meaningful violence/intimidation risk around election machinery.
guidance.3: Serious intimidation or violence risk.
guidance.4: Violence directly targets counting, certification, or transfer of power.

guidance.0: System likely converts voter preference normally.
guidance.3: Structural mismatch central to outcome.

2024.modelRead: Challenger favored because lived material stress and legitimacy/moral injury stress overpowered acceptable formal economy.
keyLessons: Do not score formal economy as lived economy.
No recession does not mean voters feel materially secure.
Contained protest can still create coalition legitimacy damage.
A nominee switch can preserve formal institutional unity while failing to restore organic legitimacy.

2020.modelRead: Incumbent collapse risk due COVID, recession shock, unrest, governance crisis, and legitimacy collapse.
keyLessons: When formal economy, lived economy, and legitimacy all collapse together, the White House party is in severe danger.
High opposition fear cannot save an incumbent when crisis performance becomes the central issue.
Democratic conversion risk should be scored separately from voter-pressure result.

2016.actualOutcome: Trump won Electoral College; Clinton won popular vote
2016.modelRead: Challenger favored in converted outcome because material/legitimacy stress and Electoral College inefficiency outweighed acceptable formal economy.
keyLessons: Formal economy can look acceptable while lived legitimacy collapses.
Elite-continuity candidate affect can intensify material grievance.
Popular mandate and Electoral College outcome must be modeled separately.
Regional conversion efficiency can decide the result.

2012.modelRead: Incumbent favored because slow recovery did not become legitimacy collapse, and Romney did not become an anti-system alternative.
keyLessons: Material pain does not automatically defeat the incumbent if voters still blame the previous governing coalition.
A credible recovery story can reduce lived-material stress.
Opposition blamed for prior crisis can offset incumbent stress.

2008.modelRead: Incumbent-party collapse because formal economy, lived economy, war fatigue, legitimacy, and candidate-affect layers all aligned against Republicans.
keyLessons: This is the clean case where old models and new model agree.
When macro collapse and lived collapse coincide, formal economic models work well.
Open-seat stress becomes severe when the outgoing administration is deeply discredited.

2004.modelRead: Vulnerable incumbent survived because war/legitimacy stress was offset by security framing and challenger weakness.
keyLessons: Foreign-policy stress can be high without defeating an incumbent if opposition threat offset is also high.
War fatigue must be scored by whether it breaks the incumbent coalition enough to change votes.
A challenger can fail to convert incumbent stress.

2000.actualOutcome: Gore won popular vote; Bush won Electoral College after Florida dispute
2000.modelRead: Incumbent party favored on popular mandate, but catastrophic democratic conversion risk and Electoral College mechanics produced Bush presidency.
keyLessons: Do not force one winner output where popular mandate and converted outcome diverge.
Tiny decisive-state margins require separate democratic conversion risk scoring.
Court intervention and ballot disputes can override normal voter-pressure logic.

1996.modelRead: Incumbent strongly favored because formal economy, lived economy, candidate affect, and opposition weakness aligned.
keyLessons: When official economy and lived economy both feel good, incumbent stress stays low.
Scandal residue only matters if it becomes broad legitimacy collapse.
Weak challenger lowers conversion risk.

1992.actualOutcome: Clinton defeated George H. W. Bush
1992.modelRead: Challenger favored because recession memory, lived insecurity, Perot anti-system pressure, and out-of-touch candidate affect created enough incumbent stress.
keyLessons: Recession memory can matter after technical recovery begins.
Third-party strength can signal anti-system pressure even if it does not win.
Candidate affect can crystallize economic grievance.

1988.actualOutcome: George H. W. Bush defeated Dukakis
1988.modelRead: Incumbent party favored because Reagan-era economy/legitimacy transferred enough to Bush.
keyLessons: Open-seat stress can be low if the outgoing incumbent is popular and continuity is credible.
A challenger who fails the affect test cannot exploit ordinary open-seat vulnerability.

1984.modelRead: Incumbent strongly favored due recovery, candidate affect, and weak challenger.
keyLessons: Strong recovery after prior pain can reset lived material stress.
Candidate charisma/affect can deepen a low-stress incumbent advantage.

1980.modelRead: Incumbent collapse because formal economy, lived material conditions, legitimacy, foreign-policy humiliation, and candidate affect all failed.
keyLessons: This is the textbook high-stress incumbent defeat.
Material stress and legitimacy stress were visible enough for older models to capture indirectly.
Primary challenge plus foreign-policy humiliation raises institutional stress sharply.

1976.modelRead: Challenger favored because Watergate legitimacy collapse, unelected incumbency, Nixon pardon, and post-Vietnam distrust overwhelmed Ford.
keyLessons: Scandal and legitimacy can dominate even when the new incumbent personally seems less corrupt.
Unelected succession raises open-seat/incumbency stress.
A pardon or elite self-protection act can preserve legitimacy damage.

1972.modelRead: Incumbent survived despite unrest and Vietnam because challenger threat offset was very high.
keyLessons: High legitimacy stress does not guarantee defeat if the challenger is successfully framed as unacceptable.
Opposition threat offset is essential for explaining elections like 1972 and 1964.

1968.modelRead: Challenger favored because Vietnam, assassinations, riots, LBJ withdrawal, convention chaos, and Wallace split created a visible legitimacy crisis.
keyLessons: This is the example of legitimacy stress becoming obvious institutional stress.
Third-party regional pressure can change conversion geography.
A strong economy cannot save a party from severe war legitimacy collapse.

1964.modelRead: Incumbent landslide because Johnson had low stress and Goldwater produced maximum opposition-threat offset.
keyLessons: A scary challenger can dramatically reduce incumbent danger.
Opposition threat offset should be high when voters perceive the challenger as outside the acceptable governing range.

1960.modelRead: Competitive/slight challenger opening due open seat, mild recession, Kennedy affect, and incomplete Eisenhower transfer.
keyLessons: A low-30s stress score should be read as competitive, not impossible for challenger.
Candidate affect can matter most in close, low-to-medium stress elections.

1956.modelRead: Incumbent landslide due national-hero affect, prosperity, and low legitimacy stress.
keyLessons: National-hero incumbency can suppress candidate-affect stress to zero.
Low stress across all layers predicts easy incumbent survival.

1952.modelRead: Challenger favored due Korea, Truman fatigue, corruption concerns, open seat, and Eisenhower national-hero challenger status.
keyLessons: A national-hero challenger reduces opposition-threat offset and raises candidate-affect stress for the incumbent party.
War fatigue and party fatigue can combine even if the economy is not the only problem.

1948.modelRead: Competitive incumbent survival despite party splits because Truman retained enough New Deal/labor legitimacy and Dewey failed to convert opposition.
keyLessons: Stress in the mid-to-high 30s is unstable, not automatic defeat.
Party splits matter, but coalition legitimacy and challenger failure can keep the incumbent alive.
Pre-1952 scoring is less precise because polling/lived-condition data is thinner.

materialStress: Score high when voters' daily household experience contradicts macroeconomic optimism.
Do not reduce lived stress just because inflation is cooling; ask whether prices, rent, and debt remain politically painful.
Use 2024 as the archetype for high lived stress with acceptable formal economy.
Use 2008 and 1980 as archetypes where formal and lived economic stress both score high.
Use 1996 and 1984 as archetypes where both formal and lived stress score low.
legitimacyStress: Score high when the incumbent party's moral claims are contradicted by war, repression, corruption, elite contempt, or coalition betrayal.
Do not require 1968-level street unrest to score legitimacy stress high.
Use 2024 as contained but electorally meaningful coalition moral injury.
oppositionThreatOffset: Score high when fear of the challenger plausibly pulls voters back toward the incumbent party.
Use 2020 and 2024 Trump as high but not identical offsets.
Use 2008 Obama and 1992 Clinton as low offset because the challenger was broadly acceptable or inspiring.
Do not score offset as agreement with the challenger; score whether the electorate found the challenger unacceptable enough to rescue the incumbent.
electoralConversion: Score high when the incumbent can win national support but lose decisive states.
Use 2016 as the strongest modern example.
Use 2000 as high conversion plus catastrophic machinery risk.
Use 2024 as lower popular-vote split risk but meaningful challenger swing-state efficiency.
Use landslides such as 1984 and 2008 as low conversion-risk elections.
democraticConversionRisk: Use 2000 as catastrophic because razor-thin state margins, ballot disputes, partisan administration, and court intervention changed the converted outcome.
Use 2020 as high because of fake-elector/certification sabotage and violence, even though the attempt failed.
Use 2016 as moderate structural mismatch but not a direct machinery breakdown.
Use normal landslides as low risk.

mistake1.error: Treating formal economy and lived economy as the same thing.
mistake1.fix: Score recession/GDP/unemployment separately from rent, groceries, debt, and worse-off sentiment.

mistake2.error: Only scoring legitimacy stress when there are riots.
mistake2.fix: Score coalition moral injury, base betrayal, and repression even if unrest is contained.

mistake3.error: Using one winner output for elections like 2000 or 2016.
mistake3.fix: Always separate popular mandate, Electoral College conversion, and democratic conversion risk.

mistake4.error: Letting personal ideology drive slider values.
mistake4.fix: Ask whether the factor plausibly affected turnout, persuasion, defection, or legitimacy.

mistake5.fix: Split the issue by political mechanism. Example: Gaza can score foreign failure, moral rupture, protest repression, and base demobilization, but each score should reflect a distinct effect.

mistake6.error: Assuming high stress always means challenger wins.
mistake6.fix: Apply opposition-threat offset. A terrifying challenger can save a weak incumbent.

analystWorkflow: Identify the White House party and score stress against that party.
Score institutional stress first because it frames incumbency, party unity, third-party pressure, and scandal.
Score formal economy using official indicators: recession, unemployment, inflation, GDP, misery index.
Score lived material conditions using voter experience: worse-off sentiment, rent, groceries, debt, housing, life milestones.
Score legitimacy and moral injury using coalition trust, protest, repression, war, hypocrisy, and donor/state capture.
Score foreign/military stress separately from moral injury.
Score candidate affect based on whether the nominee fits the crisis.
Subtract opposition threat offset based on whether the challenger is unacceptable enough to rescue the incumbent party.
Score Electoral College conversion separately from voter pressure.
Score democratic conversion risk separately from Electoral College geography.
Generate three outputs: popular mandate, converted outcome, and democratic conversion risk.
